content: It has been observed that individuals with COVID-19 who possess pre-existing autoantibodies against type I interferons are more likely to experience an inflammatory cytokine storm, which is a key driver of severe respiratory symptoms. Interleukin-6 (IL-6), a cytokine released during this inflammatory process, has been targeted with IL-6 blocking agents as a therapeutic approach for severe COVID-19 cases. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of IL-6 blocking agents compared to standard care or placebo in individuals with COVID-19. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, the Living OVerview of Evidence (L·OVE) platform, and the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, with the last search performed on June 7, 2022. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared IL-6 blocking agents to standard care or placebo, regardless of disease severity. A total of 32 trials involving 12,160 hospitalized participants were included, with an additional 17 registered RCTs identified but without available results. The mean age of participants ranged from 56 to 75 years, and 66.2% of the participants were male. One-third of the trials were placebo-controlled, and most were multicenter studies conducted between February 2020 and June 2021. The severity of COVID-19 among participants ranged from mild to critical, with varying proportions of intubated patients at baseline. Notably, only six trials reported vaccination status, and none included vaccinated participants. The review assessed six IL-6 blocking agents: tocilizumab, sarilumab, clazakizumab, siltuximab, olokizumab, and levilimab. Tocilizumab was evaluated in 20 trials, sarilumab in nine trials, and the remaining agents in one or two trials each. Two trials assessed more than one treatment. Efficacy and Safety of Tocilizumab and Sarilumab: At 28 days (D28), tocilizumab and sarilumab likely result in little to no improvement in clinical outcomes. For tocilizumab, the risk ratio (RR) was 1.05 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00 to 1.11; moderate-certainty evidence), and for sarilumab, the RR was 0.99 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.05; moderate-certainty evidence). For clinical improvement at 60 days or more (≥D60), the evidence was of very low certainty for both tocilizumab (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.48) and sarilumab (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.63). The effect of tocilizumab on reducing the proportion of participants with a WHO Clinical Progression Score (WHO-CPS) of level 7 or above at D28 is uncertain (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.12; low-certainty evidence). For sarilumab, the evidence is very uncertain (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.33; very low-certainty evidence). Tocilizumab reduces all-cause mortality at D28 compared to standard care or placebo (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.94; high-certainty evidence). However, the evidence for sarilumab's effect on this outcome is very uncertain (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.30; very low-certainty evidence). For all-cause mortality at ≥D60, the evidence is uncertain for tocilizumab (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04; low-certainty evidence) and very uncertain for sarilumab (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.07; very low-certainty evidence). Tocilizumab likely results in little to no difference in the risk of adverse events (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.12; moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence for adverse events with sarilumab is uncertain (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.28; low-certainty evidence). The evidence for serious adverse events is very uncertain for tocilizumab (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; very low-certainty evidence) and uncertain for sarilumab (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21; low-certainty evidence). Efficacy and Safety of Clazakizumab, Olokizumab, Siltuximab, and Levilimab: The evidence for these agents is derived from only one or two studies for each, and the findings are uncertain or very uncertain. Conclusions: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, tocilizumab demonstrates a beneficial effect on short-term all-cause mortality and likely results in little to no difference in the risk of adverse events compared to standard care or placebo. However, both tocilizumab and sarilumab likely result in little to no improvement in clinical outcomes at D28. The evidence for sarilumab and other IL-6 blocking agents on critical outcomes remains uncertain or very uncertain. Most trials included in this review were conducted before the emergence of different variants of concern and before widespread vaccination. Although 17 additional RCTs are registered, the number of planned participants is low, and no further updates to this review are planned.
